'''W. S. W.''' An abbreviation of ''west-southwest.''

'''wt.''' A contraction of ''weight.''

'''wudder''' (wud′ėr), ''v. i.'' See ''wuther.''

'''wude†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''wood''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wulfenite''' (wu̇l′fen-īt), ''n.'' [Named after Baron von ''Wülffen'' or ''Wülfen'' (1728–1805), an Austrian scientist.] Native lead molybdate, a mineral of a bright-yellow to orange, red, green, or brown color and resinous to adamantine luster. {{smaller|It occurs in tetragonal crystals, often in very thin tabular form, also granular massive. Also called ''yellow lead ore.''}}

'''wull.''' An obsolete or dialectal form of ''will''<sup>1</sup>, ''will''<sup>2</sup>.

'''wummel, wummle''', ''n.'' Scotch forms of ''wimble''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wun†''', ''v. i.'' See ''won''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wungee''' (wun′jē), ''n.'' [E. Ind.] A variety in India of the muskmelon, ''Cucumis Melo'', sometimes regarded as a species, ''C. cicatrisatus.'' It is of an ovate form, about 6 inches long.

'''wurali, wurari''', ''n.'' Same as ''curari.''

'''wurd†''', ''n.'' An old spelling of ''word''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wurmal†''' (wėr′mal), ''n.'' Same as ''wormal.''

'''wurrus''' (wur′us), ''n.'' [< Ar. ''wars'', a dyestuff similar to kamila.] A brick-red dye-powder, somewhat like dragon’s-blood, collected from the seeds of ''Rottlera tinctoria.''

'''wurse†, wurst†.''' Old spellings of ''worse, worst.''

'''Würtemberger''' (wėr′tem-bėrg-ėr; G. pron. vür′tem-ber-gėr), ''n.'' [< ''Würtemberg'' (G. ''Württemberg'') (see def.) + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] An inhabitant of Würtemberg, a kingdom of southern Germany.

'''Wyclifite, Wycliffite''' (wik′lif-īt), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [Also ''Wicliffite, Wickliffite''; < ''Wyclif'', etc. (see def.), + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Of or pertaining to John Wyclif or de Wyclif (a name also written ''Wiclif, Wickliffe, Wyckliffe'', and in various other ways reflecting the varying orthography of his time, properly in modern spelling ''Wickliff''), an English theologian, reformer, and translator of the Bible from the Vulgate (died 1384).

'''II.''' ''n.'' One of the followers of Wyclif, commonly called ''Lollards.'' {{smaller|Wyclif’s doctrines, propagated in his lifetime and later by open-air preachers called “poor priests,” largely coincided with the later teachings of Luther.}}

'''Wykehamist''' (wik′a̤m-ist), ''n.'' [< ''Wykeham'' (see def.) + ''-ist.''] A student, or one who has been a student, of Winchester College in England, founded by William of Wykeham (1324-1404), Bishop of Winchester and Chancellor of England, as a preparatory school for New College at Oxford, also founded by him. Also used attributively.

{{right|''Athenæum'', No. 3303, p. 212.}}}}

{{right|''Landor'', Imag. Conv., Southey and Porson, i.}}}}

'''wrymouth''' (rī′mouth), ''n.'' In ''ichth.'': (''a'') Any fish of the family ''Cryptacanthodidæ'' (which see). {{smaller|The common wrymouth is ''Cryptacanthodes maculatus'', a spotless variety of which is the ghost-fish, specified as ''C. inornatus''. It is a blennioid of slender eel-like form, normally profusely spotted, found not very commonly on the Atlantic coast of North America.}}
{{smaller block|The cod-fish, the cunner, the sea-raven, the rock-eel, and the ''wry-mouth'', which inhabit these brilliant groves, are all colored to match their surroundings.
{{right|''Science'', XV. 212.}}}}
(''b'') The electric ray, torpedo, or numb-fish. See cuts under ''Torpedinidæ'' and ''torpedo''.

'''wry-mouthed''' (rī′moutht), ''a.'' '''1.''' Having a crooked mouth; hence, unflattering.
{{smaller block|<poem>A shaggy tapestry: . . .
Instructive work! whose ''wry-mouth’d'' portraiture
Display’d the fates her confessors endure.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Dunciad, ii. 145.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''conch.'', having an irregular or distorted aperture of the shell.   ''P. P. Carpenter.''

'''wryneck''' (rī′nek), ''n.'' '''1.''' A twisted or distorted neck; a deformity in which the neck is drawn to one side and rotated. See ''torticollis''.—'''2.''' A spasmodic disease of sheep, in which the head is drawn to one side.—'''3.''' A scansorial picarian bird of the genus ''Iynx'' (''Junx'', or ''Yunx''), allied to the woodpeckers, and belonging to the same family or a closely related one: so called from the singular manner in which it can twist the neck, and so turn it awry. {{smaller|The common wryneck of Europe is ''I.'' (''J.'' or ''Y.'') ''torquilla''; there are several}} other similar species. These birds have the toes in pairs, the bill straight and hard, the tongue extremely
long, slender, and extensile, and most other characters of the true ''Picidæ'' or woodpeckers; but the tail-feathers are soft, broad, and rounded at the ends, and not used in climbing. The wryneck is migratory and insectivorous, and its general habits are similar to those of woodpeckers. It has a variety of names pointing to its arrival in the British Islands at the same time as the cuckoo, as ''cuckoo’s-fool'', ''-footman'', ''-knave'', ''-leader'', ''-maid'', ''-mate'', ''-messenger'', ''-marrow'', ''-whit'', etc. It is also called ''writheneck'' and ''snake-bird'', from the twisting of its neck; ''long-tongue'' and ''tongue-bird'', from its long tongue; ''emmet-hunter'', from feeding on ants; ''pea-bird'', ''weet-bird'', from its cry; ''turkey-bird'', ''nile-bird'', and ''slab'', for some unexplained reasons.

[[File:century v08 p0800 c1f1.png|center|249px]]
{{c|{{smaller|Common Wryneck (''Iynx torquilla'').}}}}

{{smaller block|Even while I write I hear the quaint queak, queak, queak of the ''wryneck''.
{{right|''Mortimer Collins'', Thoughts in my Garden, I. 62.}}}}

{{smaller block|The ''wryneck'' will tap the tree, to stimulate the insect to run out to be eaten entire. {{right|''P. Robinson'', Under the Sun, p. 36.}}}}

'''wry-necked''' (rī′nekt), ''a.'' Having a wry or distorted neck.
{{smaller block|<poem>When you hear the drum,
And the vile squealing of the ''wry-neck’d'' fife.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., ii. 5. 30.}}}}
{{smaller block|[By some this is understood as an allusion to the bend of the fifer’s neck while playing upon his instrument; by others (less probably) to an old form of the flute, called the ''flute-à-bec'', having a curved mouthpiece like the beak of a bird at one side.]}}
{{smaller block|A fife is a ''wry-neckt'' musician, for he always looks away from his instrument.
{{right|''Barnaby Rich'', Irish Hubbub (1616). (''Furness.'')}}}}

'''wryness''' (rī′nes), ''n.'' The state of being wry or distorted.

[Named after Dr. Henry ''Wurtz'', of New York (b. 1828).] A kind of solid bitumen found in the Uintah Mountains, Utah. {{smaller|It has a deep-black color and brilliant luster, and breaks with a conchoidal fracture. It is elastic when slightly warmed, and in boiling water becomes soft and plastic.}}

'''wurtzite''' (wėrt′sīt), ''n.''   [After C. A. ''Wurtz'' (1817–1884), a French chemist.]   Sulphid of zinc occurring in hexagonal crystals, isomorphous with greenockite. {{smaller|Sulphid of zinc is accordingly dimorphous, the common form, sphalerite or zinc-blende, being isometric. Also called ''spiauterite''.}}

'''Würzburger''' (wėrts′bėrg-ėr; G. pron. vürts′bür-gėr), ''n.'' Wine made in the neighborhood of the city of Würzburg, in Bavaria. {{smaller|This name is often given to the wines more properly called ''Leisten-wein'' and ''Stein-wein'', and to the famous “wine of the Holy Ghost.”}}

'''wus'''<sup>2</sup>†, ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''woose'', ''ooze''.
{{smaller block|Hee wringes oute the wet ''wus'' and went on his gate.
{{right|''Alisaunder of Macedoine'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 712.}}}}

'''wuther''' (wuᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''v. i.''   [Also ''wudder''; perhaps ult. < AS. ''wōth'', a noise, cry, sound.]   To make a sullen roar, as the wind. [North. Eng.]
{{smaller block|The air was now dark with snow; an Iceland blast was driving it wildly. This pair neither heard the long ''wuthering'' rush, nor saw the white burden it drifted.
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Shirley, xxiii.}}}}
{{smaller block|From time to time the wind ''wuthered'' in the chimney at his back.
{{right|''R. L. Stevenson and L. Osbourne'', The Wrong Box, vi.}}}}
{{smaller block|There was also a ''wuthering'' wind sobbing through the narrow wet streets. {{right|''A. E. Barr'', Friend Olivia, iv.}}}}

'''wuther''' (wuᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''n.''   [Also ''wudder''; < ''wuther'', ''v.'']   A low roaring or rustling, as of the wind. [North. Eng.]
{{smaller block|I felt sure . . . by the ''wuther'' of wind amongst trees, denoting a garden outside.
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Villette, xvi.}}}}

'''wuzzent''' (wuz′ẹnt), ''a.'' A dialectal (Scotch) form of ''wizened''.
{{smaller block|An I had ye amang the Frigate-Whins, wadna I set my ten talents in your ''wuzzent'' face for that very word!
{{right|''Scott'', Heart of Mid-Lothian, xviii.}}}}

'''wuzzle''' (wuz′l), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''wuzzled'', ppr. ''wuzzling''.   [Origin obscure.]   To mingle; mix; jumble; muddle. [New Eng.]
{{smaller block|He ''wuzzled'' things up in the most singular way.
{{right|''H. B. Stowe'', Oldtown, p. 63.}}}}

'''wyandotte''' (wī′an-dot), ''n.''   [From the American Indian tribal name ''Wyandotte''.]   An American variety of the domestic hen, of medium size and compact form, hardy, and valuable for eggs and for the table. {{smaller|The silver wyandotte, the typical variety, has every feather white in the middle and heavily margined with black, except the black tail-feathers and primaries, the hackle (and in males the saddle), which is white striped with black, and the white wing-bows of the males. The golden wyandotte replaces the white of the silver variety by orange or deep-buff; and the white wyandotte is pure-white. The combs are rose, legs yellow, and ear-lobes red.}}
